title: Sowing broad beans
subtitle: Autumn and spring sowing schedules for an early summer crop
excerpt: Broad beans are sown in October or November for the earliest summer crop, or in February to April for a slightly later one. The hardy seeds tolerate UK winters outdoors and germinate reliably in cold soil.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section on beans. RHS broad bean growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Joy Larkcom, Grow Your Own Vegetables, public-domain passages on sowing schedules and overwintering.

glossaryTerms.definition: Growing a plant through the winter months, either in the ground or under protection. Broad beans sown in autumn overwinter as small seedlings, resume growth in February, and crop earlier than spring-sown plants because they have a root system already established.

Removing the soft growing tip of a broad bean plant once it reaches full height and the lowest pods are forming. This removes the aphid-attractive new growth and concentrates the plant's energy into filling the existing pods.

content.text: Broad beans are the cold-season staple of the UK kitchen garden. Sow in October or November and the plants

as small seedlings, ready to surge in late February and crop in May and June. Sow in February to April and crop follows in June and July. The seeds are large enough to handle individually and push into the soil without tools.

Autumn sowing runs from late October to mid-November. The cue is soil temperature: once the ground drops below 10°C the seeds germinate slowly but surely over two to four weeks. The plants sit as 10 cm seedlings through December and January, then put on growth fast once days lengthen in February. Aquadulce Claudia is the standard autumn variety in the UK.

Spring sowing opens in February in the south of England, March in the north, and continues to late April. The soil needs to reach at least 5°C for reliable germination, which it will do in most UK gardens by late February. Spring-sown plants catch up quickly and crop two to three weeks behind autumn-sown ones.

Direct sow into the ground or into large modules to transplant later. In waterlogged ground or heavy clay, modules give a better start: sow into 9 cm pots of multi-purpose compost, germinate on a cool windowsill or unheated greenhouse, and transplant at 8 to 10 cm tall. Broad beans need full sun and a reasonably fertile, well-drained soil. They do poorly in waterlogged spots.

Sow 5 cm deep, one seed every 20 cm, in double rows 20 cm apart. Leave 60 cm between double rows so you can reach in to pick. A dibber, a trowel handle, or a finger makes a clean hole. Push the seed in, close the hole, water once. The seeds are large enough that birds will sometimes dig them up in the first few days; a fine net over the bed prevents this.

Broad bean seedlings push up as two thick seed leaves followed immediately by the first true leaves. Germination takes one to three weeks in autumn soil, seven to ten days in a warm spring. If nothing has shown after three weeks, the seed has probably rotted. Autumn-sown seed sometimes rots in wet years; re-sow in February without dismay.

Autumn-sown plants need no care over winter beyond keeping the bed weed-free. Tall varieties may need support: put in canes at either end of each double row and run string between them once plants reach 30 cm. Dwarf varieties (The Sutton) need no support.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: Four issues that crop up most often with broad beans.

items.cause: Black bean aphid (Aphis fabae) is attracted to the new growth at the plant tip.
items.fix: Pinch out the tip and compost it. Rub off any clusters you can see with your fingers. Ladybirds and hoverfly larvae will follow if you give them a week. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides which kill the predators.

items.symptom: Plants lean over or fall down in wind
items.cause: Tall varieties without support, particularly on exposed plots.
items.fix: Run string support between canes along each side of the double row. Stake individual plants that fall away from the row.

items.symptom: Autumn-sown plants rot at the base over winter
items.cause: Waterlogged soil or an unusually wet mild winter encouraging fungal rot.
items.fix: Improve drainage before the next autumn sow: fork compost or grit into heavy clay soil. Raise the bed by 10 cm if the site sits wet.

items.symptom: Pods form but remain thin and empty
items.cause: Poor pollination or a very dry spell at pod-set.
items.fix: Water consistently once pods form. Broad beans are bee-pollinated; if no bees are visiting, plant borage or phacelia nearby to attract them.
